title: The benefits of full data shuffle, now with optimal I/O cost: $k$-wise independence and matrix transposition to the rescue
claim: Naive or partial shuffles leave visible structure in input-output position; our method gives a permutation that looks uniformly random.
layout: 6 scatter panels in 2x3 grid, shared axes, reading left-to-right then down
description: A 2x3 grid of scatter plots titled 'Visualization of shuffle behavior'. Every panel plots input position (x, 0–1000) against output position (y, 0–1000) for one shuffle algorithm, all in the same blue dots. The top row shows No shuffle, which is a perfect diagonal line. Next is IO shuffle with 1 round, which gives horizontal blocky clusters. Third is CorgiPile, which gives smaller but still visible horizontal streaks. The bottom row shows Fisher-Yates, a uniform random cloud. Next is IO shuffle with 2 rounds, which looks nearly uniform. Last is Gen-2-wise-Ind-Perm, a regular lattice of dots with diagonal structure. The shared axis labels sit on the outer left and bottom. The eye goes first to the contrast between the straight diagonal line and the dense random clouds.
caption: Visualization of shuffle algorithms. Each algorithm is executed once on an input with block size B = 14 and N = 1013
abstract: It is known that RandomShuffle, the without replacement version of Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD), converges faster than with replacement SGD. However, RandomShuffle requires uniformly performing a random permutation of the input sequence, which is known to have high I/O complexity due to data movement across the memory hierarchy. In this paper, we propose a shuffling algorithm with a linear I/O complexity that generates almost-uniformly random permutations with rigorous mathematical guarantees. Specifically, we show that the shuffling algorithm can generate $2$-wise independent permutations. Furthermore, we can extend to $k$-wise independence with a small error in the probability distribution, if the fast memory has at least $k$ memory blocks. These results allow us to reach the same expected theoretical convergence as RandomShuffle while achieving optimal linear I/O cost.
